On-connect commands

Sent once, after ShellMate has identified the device and turned paging off. One line per prompt, each echoed into the session as though you had typed it, and the whole script announced before anything goes out.

Up to 12 lines. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. A destructive command still stops and asks, exactly as one you typed would. Saved with the connection, so it runs every time — a connection you have not saved yet gets it from the next time you open it.

Typed at the Password: an enable line produces, and nowhere else. Kept in the encrypted vault with your other credentials — never in profiles.json, and never sent back to this dialog. Leave it blank to keep the one already saved.

Output Colours

Colour terminal text by pattern, so the line that matters stands out of a wall of output. Patterns are regular expressions.

Device Awareness

On connect, ShellMate works out what it is talking to — from the login banner, or failing that from the shape of the prompt — and adapts to it. Both settings below depend on that succeeding confidently. A banner naming the software is conclusive; a prompt on its own usually is not, because hostname(config)# is printed identically by IOS, NX-OS, ASA and EOS, and they do not share a paging command. When ShellMate is not sure, it sends nothing at all rather than guess, and says so in the corner of the terminal.

That case is common — a legal banner replacing the version string, or a device reached through a terminal server. When it happens, click the device name in the status bar and say what it is; both settings then apply immediately.

s

Sends the right command for the platform — terminal length 0, terminal pager 0, set cli screen-length 0 — so no more --More--. It is echoed like anything you typed, never sent silently. Off, or unidentified, means paging stays as the device left it.

Type ints and get the right interface command for whatever you are connected to. Only a bare alias on its own is expanded, and the terminal shows what was actually sent.

Platform Definitions

What ShellMate knows about each kind of device: which command turns paging off, how to fetch the running config, and the aliases available on it. Adding a platform here is how ShellMate learns a device it has never seen.

These are stored as platforms.json in your data folder, and this editor writes that file. Editing it by hand is worth knowing about for bulk changes, or to carry your definitions to another machine — delete it to restore the built-in set.

Leave blank to send nothing on connect.

Comma-separated text found in the device's banner or version output. The longest match wins, so be specific.

Type the short name and get the command. Only a bare alias on its own is expanded, and the terminal shows what was actually sent.

These live in ShellMate, not on the device. The expansion happens here before anything is sent, so nothing is configured on the device, nothing persists there after you disconnect, and the same alias works across every device of this platform — including ones you have never logged into. Somebody using a different tool on the same switch sees none of this.

SSH & Serial

Starting values for a new serial connection, so the same settings are not re-entered every time. Cisco console is 9600 8-N-1 with no flow control.

Credentials Vault

API keys and remembered device passwords are encrypted on disk — unless you asked for a particular one to be kept as readable text, which the list below marks and lets you undo.

Status Checking…

Backup and restore

A backup is the whole vault under a passphrase you choose, so it can be carried to another machine or another Windows account. The file holds every API key and remembered device password — keep it as carefully as you would the vault itself.

Shared credentials

A login several connections use. They point at it rather than each keeping a copy, so changing it here fixes every device using it.

Saved device credentials

Session Logging

Masks credentials in written logs — devices echo, and a session log is meant to be handed to someone else. The terminal itself always shows the truth.

A relative name goes in your data folder; an absolute path is used as given, so a network share works.

Configuration Capture

On connect, ShellMate fetches the device's running configuration and keeps it, so every login becomes a change check with nothing to remember. It prefers a second channel — invisible, never in the session you are typing in. Where the device refuses one, or the transport cannot carry one at all, it can fall back to your own session; that fallback has its own switch below and always says afterwards what it did.

Where a second channel is refused — serial and telnet cannot open one, and some switches allow only one session at a time — it can fall back to running the command through your own session: only while it sits idle at a prompt, hidden from the screen and the transcript, and announced afterwards. The fallback has its own switch below, for anyone who wants captures on a second channel or not at all.

Files are masked by the same “Obscure passwords and secrets” setting above — a running configuration carries hashes, keys and community strings, and this folder may well be a share.

Kept apart from session logs on purpose: a capture is a thing as it was, a log is a record of what you did. A relative name goes in your data folder; an absolute path is used as given, so a network share works.

The system prompts — what the assistant is told before it sees anything of yours — are in Stockton, under AI assistant.

API keys and endpoints. Keys are stored in the encrypted vault above; anything saved here overrides the matching .env variable. Leaving a field empty falls back to .env.

Optional. When set, ShellMate queries this Chroma collection on every chat for design-guideline snippets and injects matches into the AI prompt. Leave blank to disable.

Not tested

The system prompts

What the assistant is told before it sees anything of yours. These are the largest single influence on how it answers, and they are yours to change — tell it to stop explaining things you already know, to always mention a change reference, or to answer in a house style.

Stored as prompts.json in your data folder, so they can be edited by hand, kept in version control or carried to another machine. Delete the file to restore the shipped text.

Alerts

ShellMate watches for things that will happen to a device unless someone intervenes — reload in 10, or a Junos commit confirmed waiting to be confirmed. The countdown on the tab and in the status bar is always shown; these control how loudly it interrupts you.

Over the last five minutes only. A tab that pulses for ten minutes is one people stop seeing.

A short tone at ten minutes, five, one and ten seconds. Synthesised in the browser, so it works with no network at all.

The one that reaches you when you are looking at a different tab. Click it to jump to the device. The last warning stays until dismissed.

Replaces the flashing with a steady outline. Your system setting is honoured too.

Broadcast

Send a command, or a sequence, to several devices at once. The command library — saved snippets, vendor groups, the quick-broadcast bolt — lives in the Broadcast panel itself, not here; these rows only govern its pacing and safety.

Ansible

ShellMate does not run Ansible. It drives an ansible-runner-service container over its REST API and shows what that container is doing. The service authenticates with a client certificate rather than a token, so a certificate and its key are what it needs — as paths on this machine, never as text stored here.

s

Licence

ShellMate works without a licence. A licence lets it update itself from inside the application. Keys are verified on this machine; nothing about your devices is sent anywhere. Need one? Request a key, or write to support@foundry-ns.com.

SSH Keys

        
      


      

        

          
Create a key

          
Ed25519 unless something refuses it — smaller, faster, and the modern default. The private half never leaves this machine.


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          


          

            
            
          

        


        

          
Import an existing key

          
Copied in rather than referenced, so the list means one thing and the permissions can be tightened. A key left where it is still works through the connection dialog.


          

            

              
              
              
            

          

        


        
        

          
Inspect a certificate

          
Paste an OpenSSH certificate — the whole line from a *-cert.pub file — or an X.509 certificate, the TLS kind a device serves on its management page, between its BEGIN CERTIFICATE lines. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere; it is read here and reported below.

          
          

            
            
          

          

        


        

          
Your keys

          
Kept in , so they travel with your data folder. On Windows the file permissions are tightened as each is written — OpenSSH refuses a private key other accounts can read.

          

        


        
        

          
Known hosts

          
The host keys ShellMate has trusted, in . A device is trusted the first time you reach it; if its key ever changes after that, the connection stops and asks. Forget makes the next connection to that device a first connection — use it after a genuine replacement you would rather not be asked about again.

          
Your own ~/.ssh/known_hosts is read as well and never written to, so a device OpenSSH already trusts is not asked about here.

          

        

      

    

  


  
  
  

    

      

        
Find Devices

        
      


      

        

          info
          This makes real connections to every address you give it. That
          traffic is logged by the network, and scanning something you do not
          own or have permission to test is at best poor manners. ShellMate
          reads what each device announces and nothing more — it never tries a
          password.
        


        

          
What to scan


          

            
            
            
A subnet (10.20.30.0/24),
              a range (10.20.30.1-60), a comma-separated list, or a
              single address.

            

          


          

            
            
            
Port 22 is the one that matters:
              its banner is what tells ShellMate what the device is. Concurrency,
              timeouts and the size limit live in Stockton.

          


          

            
            
            
          


          

            

            

          

        


        

          
Found

          

            Nothing scanned yet. Only addresses that answered on a port are
            listed — a page of "nothing here" would bury the ones that did.

          


          

            
            
            
            
            
          

        


        

          
Why there is no ping

          
A ping sweep needs raw sockets, which
            need administrator rights on Windows — and ShellMate deliberately
            requires none. It would also find less: ICMP is filtered on most
            management networks, which are exactly the ones worth scanning. A
            TCP connect to port 22 needs no privileges and tells you more.

        

      

    

  


  

    

      

        
Contact Support

        
      


      

        

          
What happened?

          
What you were doing, and what happened instead. This goes in the bundle as a plain text file.

          

            
          

        


        

          
What to include

          
Nothing is gathered unless you tick it, and Preview shows exactly what would be written. API keys, device passwords and vault contents are never collected at all.

          

        


        

          
Just want to say something?

          
An idea, something that reads oddly, a device that behaved unexpectedly, or that it is useful — all welcome, and none of it needs a diagnostic bundle. Opens an email with nothing attached.
